messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas, a 71‑year‑old insurance agent, has lived with the echoes of a brutal childhood for most of his life. When he was ten, his caregiver—who had long been drunk—hitted him until his ribs ached and then left him locked in the back closet for hours. The night of that assault still rattles him: the sudden clang of sirens outside his home feels like the wail of the caretaker’s curses, strangers in the hallway remind him of the caregiver’s looming threat, and the faint scent of alcohol at a bar brings the smell of that night to the surface. Each trigger brings a vivid flash of the memory, the image of his body bruised and trembling, the sudden, fragmented pieces that appear without warning and then vanish, and a feeling that his memories are more real than any ordinary recollection. The sense of betrayal that he was left to endure with no one ever held accountable floods his mind, and he feels his body has become a weapon of its own—always reacting as if danger lurks around the corner. This negative appraisal turns the ordinary sound of a siren into a harbinger of threat, and the mere sight of a stranger makes him hyper‑aware of potential danger. The persistent sense of threat has made Thomas constantly vigilant. He spends hours at his desk listening for the creak of a hallway, watching the windows for the flash of a passing car, and rehearsing mental rituals that he believes will shield him from harm. When he hears a siren, his mind leaps back to the night of abuse, reinforcing his conviction that no one was ever held accountable and that he must never trust. The fear that strangers might appear as the caretaker once did keeps him on edge, while the sudden appearance of a memory when a siren blares triggers an acute sense of danger. Each perceived threat pulls him into a mental dance of distraction and ritual, a way to stave off the pounding in his chest and the nagging belief that his body will betray him again. The fear that the world is full of hidden danger fuels his intrusive monitoring, and that monitoring in turn makes him more sensitive to every new trigger. Thomas’s coping strategies are woven tightly into the fabric of his memories. Whenever a fragment of his childhood flashes—whether the smell of alcohol, a passing stranger, or the sudden crack of a siren—he immediately launches into a mental ritual: he imagines a shield around his body, mentally repeats phrases that promise safety, and then flings his attention to the next task, a way to keep his mind occupied. These strategies reinforce his negative appraisal that no one will ever be held accountable; by repeatedly convincing himself that he can ward off harm, he also convinces himself that the threat is always real. Yet the very act of rehearsing protection deepens his sense of threat, because each successful rehearsal reminds him that the danger still exists and must be actively defended against. At work, Thomas’s world is punctuated by the same triggers. When a stranger knocks on his office door to request a policy quote, he feels the same betrayal he felt in the closet; the sudden sound of a siren outside the building sends him into a state of heightened arousal, his heart pounding, his mind racing through the violent night. The office coffee’s faint aroma, mingled with a neighbor’s laughter, reminds him of the caretaker’s drunkenness and sends a shiver down his spine. In these moments he quickly recites his mental rituals, then distracts himself with a spreadsheet, and he steers clear of any television or online news that might remind him of similar violent events. Even the simple act of closing the office door feels like a preventive ritual, as if he can physically block the threat from entering his safe space. The decision to seek help came after a false alarm when a neighbor’s loud shout at midnight caused Thomas to jump from his chair and almost fall out of bed. He realized that the anxiety was no longer just a response to real danger but had become a constant companion, draining his energy and isolating him from colleagues and friends. He fears that his body will again betray him, that his memory will surge and that the relentless threat he feels will never ease. What he hopes for is a way to quiet the inner voice that says “no one will ever hold you accountable” and to learn to trust that the world around him is not as hostile as his past has made it appear.
